items.question: The Spanish Heir (What If Carlos II had a son?)
human_answers: I'm very interested to see how the Habsburgs continue to manage their Mediterranean and American possessions. It might be too much to hope for, but perhaps if the final decades of his reign are less frantic, he might be a little more relaxed and not outlaw the use of Nahuatl and Quechua within the administration of the American colonies. Beyond that, continuing spanish rivalry with France will be interesting- I'd assume if Spain can get it's act together they'll be looking for a return of the franche comté. But as they're not as much of a land power as Austria, they might end up losing Belgium to France. Corsica and Tuscany are also up for grabs this century, which could confirm them as masters of all Italy. In the Mediterranean, Spanish support might lead to a longer lasting Catholic Morea, whether under the Venetians or under the Spanish themselves- and given how much the spanish the like Catholicism, it might scare the orthodox within the ottoman empire into closer association with the ottoman state. Austrian-ottoman wars in the beginning of the 18th century will be altered should the Spanish coordinate with their cousins by sea- Crete, Cyprus and even Rhodes could be targets here. The age of dynastic partitions is mainly over, but one more might just be on the cards- either Castile and the colonies Vs Aragon and the Mediterranean, or Spain and the colonies Vs Italy and the Mediterranean.

Interesting introduction and POD. I love the depiction of the Battle of Vienna that allows to put some background and context for the beginning of this thread, but also creates symbolism with a "Holy Day" for the Habsburg House. It will prevent the Spanish Sucession War (or at least, delaying it for many decades as I suspect a surviving heir and sucessor for Carlos II for this thread) and many of its aftermath (for example, the true thrive of Great Britain as it was during this war they acquired Gibraltar). Carlos II's heir would however have to face the quandary his kingdom is confronted to as it was during Carlos II's reign that the decline of Spain truly began. He would however rely on the old age of Louis XIV when he will be of age to rule, which could be helpful as France remains a powerful rival and neighbour (and I spoke of it as a Frenchman).

I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.

If Charles II of Spain (Carlos II), who died childless in 1700, had produced a healthy, surviving son, the entire course of early eighteenth‑century European history would likely have shifted dramatically.

The central cause of the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) was the extinction of the Spanish Habsburg line. Charles’s death without an heir triggered competing claims from the Bourbon dynasty of France (through Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV) and the Austrian Habsburgs (through Archduke Charles). European powers feared that either outcome would upset the balance of power—especially the possibility of a Bourbon union of France and Spain. If Charles II had left a legitimate son, that immediate dynastic crisis would almost certainly have been avoided.

Assuming this son was widely recognized as legitimate and physically capable of ruling, he would have inherited the Spanish monarchy and its vast empire—Spain, Spanish Italy, the Spanish Netherlands, and the American colonies—under the continuity of the Spanish Habsburg line. This would likely have prevented the War of the Spanish Succession altogether, or at least prevented it in the form it took. France and Austria would have had far weaker legal claims, and other powers such as England and the Dutch Republic would have had less justification to intervene militarily.

However, stability would not have been guaranteed. Spain in 1700 was economically weakened, administratively strained, and militarily diminished. A son raised under Spanish Habsburg institutions might have attempted reform, but he would also have faced powerful court factions—pro-French and pro-Austrian—that had already formed around the succession issue. Foreign powers would likely have tried to influence his regency if he inherited as a minor. If he were a child at Charles II’s death, a regency period could have become a proxy struggle among European states, potentially leading to limited wars or diplomatic crises rather than a full continental conflict.

In the broader European balance of power, the absence of a Bourbon takeover of Spain would have significantly weakened France’s strategic position compared to what it briefly gained under Philip V. The Bourbon dynastic link between France and Spain—which later shaped eighteenth‑century geopolitics—would not have formed. Britain might not have acquired Gibraltar and Minorca (which it gained in the historical peace settlement), altering its Mediterranean strategy. Austria might not have gained territories in Italy and the Spanish Netherlands, changing Habsburg influence in Central Europe and Italy.

Over the longer term, a continued Spanish Habsburg dynasty might have preserved a more conservative imperial structure in Spain’s American colonies. The Bourbon Reforms of the eighteenth century—administrative, fiscal, and military centralization measures—might never have occurred or would have taken a different form. That could have delayed or altered the conditions that later contributed to Latin American independence movements.

In summary, if Charles II had had a son, the War of the Spanish Succession in its historical form would likely have been avoided, the Bourbon dynasty might never have ruled Spain, and the European balance of power in the eighteenth century would have developed along a more Habsburg‑centered axis. While Spain would still have faced deep structural challenges, the geopolitical map of Europe—and perhaps the trajectory of its global empires—would have been significantly different.

VICE PRESIDENT JOHNSON CLINGING TO LIFE IN HIS HOTEL ROOM SURROUNDED BY FAMILY! New York Herald April 15th with it's infamous Triple Headlines ​ "The death of Seward was found out relatively quickly. He died almost immediately following the stabbings at somewhere around 10:12 the night of April 14th. Over the next ten minutes, both the president and vice president would be mortally wounded. Most congressmen present in D.C. and cabinet members would be awoken around 11:00. The timeline gets confusing around here. We know that at 1:00 AM many members of Congress convened to figure out who would succeed Lincoln, should Johnson not survive. It is not known when a consensus was reached. What is known is that there was bitter debate between many figures over whether it was to be the Senate Pro Tempore Lafayette S. Foster or the Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. From a couple of memoirs, however, we can gather it was never a real debate; most people there thought the radical republicans were just complaining. To them, it was natural that the head of the Senate should assume the presidency; it's the 'upper house,' of course. That said, the radical view was that Colfax ought to be president because he was the Speaker of the People's House. Eventually bringing the 1792 Succession Act forth settled the discussion ; it became clear that the Foster faction won out. From what I was able to gather, this happened sometime between 3:00 and 6:00 AM. To appease the radicals, however, a special election would be held in November to ensure the people don't have a president no one voted for. At 7:22 in the morning, President Lincoln was pronounced dead. The next day, on the 17th, as Johnson's doctors made it clearer to Congress that he wouldn't make it, preparations were made to swear in Foster. The congressmen who weren't in the initial meeting were promptly informed of the line of succession around noon on the 17th. The next day's newspapers announced to the people that Foster would be sworn in should Johnson die. At 3:44 AM on April 19th, Vice President Johnson died. At 4:24 the same morning, Lafayette S. Foster became the 17th president of the United States. (Some circles like to say that he is actually the 18th president because Johnson was president for two days, yet that is false, as Johnson was never sworn in.) Instead, those two days simply had no president at all.)" items.original_question: Triple Calamity: What if the Three Most Important Men in the Executive Branch Died in One Night? I have never written a timeline on this site. I've read a lot of other people's timelines and I have greatly enjoyed american political history, but I never thought my knowledge base was large enough or my writing skills good enough to try my hand at writing a timeline. That said on my own in a google document I wrote an alternate history timeline (or at least a basic outline of one) for my own enjoyment. I actually think it's pretty good and I'm willing to share it. Don't feel shy to tell me if something is unrealistic, chilched or doesn't make any sense I'd be more than happy to revise and or go more in depth. Triple Calamity has the POD of George Atzerodt not losing his nerve and Lewis Powell directing his stab just a bit better. Thus Lincoln, Johnson and Seward all die on the same day. I'm sure many of you american history nerds had guessed that by the title. It's a relatively popular hypothetical I gather, but I didn't know that when I started writing . Take this as my twist. Thank you to everyone who might take their time to read my senario! Hope I can pump updates out in a timely manner! If the president, vice president, and the next highest executive officer in the line of succession (typically the Speaker of the House) all died in one night, the United States would face a moment of shock and instability, but there is a constitutional framework designed to handle exactly this kind of catastrophe.

Under the Presidential Succession Act, after the vice president, the line of succession continues to the Speaker of the House, then the president pro tempore of the Senate, followed by the Cabinet secretaries in a specified order beginning with the secretary of state. If the top three figures in the executive line were killed simultaneously, the next eligible official in that statutory order would be sworn in as president.

The transition would likely occur very quickly. The Constitution requires the new president to take the oath of office, but it does not require a public ceremony; it could be administered immediately by a judge. Continuity-of-government plans are specifically designed for scenarios involving mass-casualty events, including nuclear attacks or terrorism, and secure facilities and communication systems are in place to ensure that someone in the line of succession can assume authority without delay.

In the short term, there would be intense political and financial instability. Markets would likely react sharply, national security forces would go on high alert, and the military would elevate readiness in case the deaths were the result of foreign attack. Intelligence agencies would prioritize determining whether the event was accidental, domestic terrorism, or an act of war. Public anxiety would be high, especially if the cause were unclear.

Legally, however, the government would continue to function. The Constitution does not limit how far down the succession line authority can pass, as long as the statutory requirements are met. The new president would serve the remainder of the term unless removed or replaced through normal constitutional processes. If both the presidency and vice presidency were vacant, the new president could nominate a vice president under the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, subject to confirmation by both houses of Congress.

The greatest risk would not be constitutional breakdown but political legitimacy and national unity. If the catastrophe were tied to political violence, it could deepen polarization. If it were a foreign attack, it could trigger rapid military or diplomatic escalation. Yet structurally, the system is designed to survive even a “decapitation” event.

In short, while such a “triple calamity” would produce shock, fear, and possibly global instability, the constitutional succession framework is specifically intended to prevent a power vacuum. The United States would almost certainly continue functioning under a new president within hours.

items.original_question: What if Umar ibn Hafsun defeats the Umayyads - Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus One of my favorite historical subjects to research is Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled realms of the Iberian peninsula that existed between the 8th and 15th centuries. A land where East met West, Al-Andalus represented a rare example of Islamic Arab rule of Western European territory, resulting in the blending of cultures, religion, knowledge, and languages that proved to be massively influential on the development of European civilization and human history as a whole. Even though it was swept out of Iberia by the Reconquista, the influence of Al-Andalus can still be felt today, through Hispanic language, culture, art, and cuisine. For example, there are many Arabic loanwords in the Spanish language, tacos have middle eastern roots, and I remember a story my grandfather would tell me about when he met Bedouin tribesmen while deployed as a U.S. Marine during the Gulf War, and while they could not understand the English language, they could understand his Spanish. In the late 9th century, the once-Caliphs of the entire Muslim world, the Arab Umayyad dynasty, ruled over the vast majority of the Iberian peninsula from the prosperous city of Cordoba. Their rule would last for 300 years, but would not be without resistance. Although they comprised a small portion of the population, the ruling class of Al-Andalus was almost exclusively Arab. Mozarabs, local Iberians who remained Christian under Muslim rule, and Muladí, Iberians who had converted to Islam, resented the discriminatory racial and taxation policies of their Arab overlords, creating a degree of instability within Al-Andalus. Born around 850, Umar ibn Hafsun was a prominent leader of Iberian resistance to Umayyad rule. Simultaneously described as being of both North African and Visigothic descent, the rogue-ish and opportunistic ibn Hafsun attracted a following of disaffected Mozarab and Muladí alike, and alongside fellow rebels such as ibn Marwan and the Banu Qasi clan, would contest Umayyad rule from his fortress, Bobastro. While he would experience much success early on, several defeats against the Umayyads, such as at the Battle of Poley in 891, as well as his conversion to Christianity in 899, in what appeared to be a bid to attract the support of the Christian King of Asturias, would weaken his following. He would fight to the very end, dying in 917, and his sons would continue his fight until 928, when Bobastro fell to Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III. Umar ibn Hafsun remains somewhat of a tragic figure in Iberian history, but he also represents a glimpse into what could have been. Had he succeeded in supplanting the minority Arab ruling class with Mozarabs and Muladí, perhaps by winning battles such as the Battle of Poley, ibn Hafsun could have ensured the creation of a stronger, multicultural and multireligious Al-Andalus. This creates an interesting scenario for speculation. Could this alt-Andalus survive for longer, perhaps even to the present? What would the society of alt-Andalus look like? Would religious and ethnic differences eventually shatter this state, or would it strengthen it, combining the best of the Christian and Islamic worlds? Would alt-Andalus fall to neighboring Christian and Muslim invaders, or would it become one of the leading powers in Europe and the Mediterranean, an even greater conduit for the exchange of trade, knowledge, and culture than the Al-Andalus of OTL? And how would this alt-Andalus impact the development of Hispanic culture, and European and world history as a whole?

If Umar ibn Hafsun had decisively defeated the Umayyads in the late 9th or early 10th century and consolidated power, al-Andalus would likely have evolved into a very different political and religious entity—less centralized, less Arab-dominated, and potentially more Mozarabic and Muladí in character.

Umar ibn Hafsun himself was a Muladí (a local Iberian convert to Islam) who eventually converted to Christianity and allied with Mozarabs (Christians living under Muslim rule). His revolt drew support from marginalized groups: Muladí converts resentful of Arab-Berber elite dominance, Mozarabs burdened by taxation and discrimination, and local strongmen resisting Córdoba’s centralization. If he had succeeded in overthrowing the Umayyads, the Arab aristocratic monopoly on political power would have been broken much earlier.

Politically, al-Andalus might have fragmented into a confederation of semi-autonomous regions under local lords loyal to Ibn Hafsun or his successors, rather than developing into the highly centralized Caliphate of Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman III. The sophisticated bureaucratic and courtly culture that characterized 10th-century Córdoba may never have reached its historical peak. Instead, power would likely have been more regional, with Bobastro—Hafsun’s stronghold—becoming the symbolic center rather than Córdoba.

Religiously, the outcome would be especially significant. If Hafsun maintained his Christian allegiance after victory, al-Andalus might have shifted toward a Christian-ruled but religiously mixed polity—something akin to a reverse convivencia, where Muslims became a powerful minority rather than the ruling elite. Alternatively, even if Islam remained dominant, it would probably have taken on a more local, Iberianized character, less tied to Arab identity and Abbasid cultural models. The sharp ethnic hierarchy privileging Arabs over Berbers and Muladís would likely have eroded more rapidly.

In terms of Christian-Muslim relations across Iberia, a Hafsunid state might have blurred the frontier between al-Andalus and the northern Christian kingdoms. Diplomatic and dynastic alliances with Asturias-León or Navarre could have deepened, possibly slowing or reshaping the Reconquista. Rather than a clear civilizational and religious frontier, Iberia might have seen more hybrid polities and shifting loyalties.

Internationally, without a strong Umayyad emirate—and later caliphate—al-Andalus would have been weaker in projecting power across the western Mediterranean. The Umayyad claim to caliphal authority in 929 would likely never have occurred, reducing Iberia’s role as a rival center of Islamic legitimacy against the Abbasids and Fatimids.

In summary, a victory by Umar ibn Hafsun would probably have produced a more decentralized, socially leveling, and culturally hybrid al-Andalus. The dominance of Arab elites and the later golden age of Umayyad Córdoba might never have emerged, replaced instead by a Mozarab–Muladí-led polity that reshaped the religious and ethnic balance of medieval Iberia.

Containing The Interval Of Three Years CHAPTER I How Herod Was Slain By Caesar's Command at Rhodes And How Agrippa Led An Expedition Against Alexander and Aristobolus Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa ​ After the defeat at Actium, when Antony’s fleet was scattered and his legions deserted him, Octavian stood as the undisputed master of the Roman world. He did not return immediately to Italy but remained at Rhodes, where he received embassies from kings who had formerly supported Antony and Cleopatra. The rulers of Cappadocia, Galatia, Paphlagonia, Media Atropatene, Armenia, Commagene, Pontus, and Comana sought pardon by offering gifts and tribute. Octavian’s health, which was often fragile, had been weakened by the campaign. He was prone to illness in times of strain, and the war had aggravated this condition. At the same time, Italy demanded attention. Heavy taxation to fund the fleet and legions had caused unrest in several towns, and soldiers were increasingly insistent that their long-promised rewards of land and pay be delivered. At this moment Herod, king of the Jews, came to Rhodes to seek an audience. He argued that Judea was a useful link between Syria and Egypt, that he alone could restrain his people, and that his rule preserved the appearance of independence while ensuring obedience. Octavian rejected these arguments. He replied that Judea could be reduced to a province and governed by a Roman official. When Herod pressed his case further, Octavian reminded him of his loyalty to Antony and declared such conduct unpardonable. Herod appealed to the memory of his father Antipater’s loyalty to Julius Caesar, but Octavian dismissed the plea, noting that Antony too had once been a friend of Caesar before turning against him. Herod, recognizing that his throne was lost, asked only for his life and that of his family, offering the treasury of Judea in return for estates in Italy. Octavian refused. Herod was executed, denied the honors of a king. His wives were taken captive. His eldest son, Antipater schemed a plan and took his two half brothers, Alexander and Aristobolus, sons of Herod's second wife Mariamne, with him. They fled towards Judea. Octavian ordered Marcus Agrippa to march against them, subdue the country, and decide its future. Opinion among his advisors was divided. Some argued Judea should be annexed and governed as a province, like Egypt after the fall of the Ptolemies. Others preferred that a native ruler be appointed under Roman authority, believing this better to restrain a turbulent people and prevent disorder in greater Syria. Agrippa first made his way through Asia Minor, where he gathered soldiers from the client kingdoms and strengthened the coastal garrisons. Amyntas of Galatia, eager to prove his loyalty after previously aligning himself with Antony, sent large numbers of Galatian infantry. These were hardy men, accustomed to mountain warfare, and fought with long shields and spears in the Celtic manner, often serving Rome as mercenaries. From Archelaus of Cappadocia came contingents of light cavalry, skilled at swift raids across the plains, together with slingers and javelin-men drawn from the hill tribes. Deiotarus of Paphlagonia furnished additional horsemen, small in number but valued for their endurance in rough country. Polemon of Pontus contributed archers from the Black Sea coast, as well as light-armed troops familiar with skirmishing in wooded terrain. The Lycian League, though reluctant, yielded auxiliaries and a few ships, for Agrippa made it clear that refusal would mean the loss of their cherished autonomy and absorption into direct Roman rule. By these means Agrippa’s force swelled to nearly twenty-five thousand men, drawn from diverse peoples but bound together under Roman discipline and command. Crossing the Taurus mountains into Cilicia, Agrippa met Quintus Didius, governor of Syria. Didius furnished five thousand men, many of them veterans who had fought in the eastern campaigns under both Antony and earlier commanders. Though their loyalties had been divided in the past, Agrippa secured their service with promises of land and pay in Octavian’s name. He reviewed them in the plain, commending their experience and reminding them that the struggle was not against the Jewish nation, but against two reckless youths who disturbed the peace. From Cilicia he advanced into Syria. The great cities sent delegations: Antioch contributed money and supplies from its considerable wealth; Apamea sent its cavalry, long trained in maneuvers and valuable for pursuit; Syllaeus, the Nabataean toparch governing Damascus provided infantry levies and stores of grain. Local dynasts added archers from the hill country and slingers from the towns, while Arab chiefs along the desert frontier furnished light cavalry skilled in raiding and ambush. Thus Agrippa found no shortage of auxiliaries. Fear that Judea’s unrest might disturb Syria moved each city to support Rome, for the Jews themselves were not in rebellion against Caesar, but were troubled by the ambition of Herod’s sons. When he had mustered them at the Roman colony of Berytus, Agrippa addressed the assembly. He reminded them of Rome’s victories, how Antony and Cleopatra had fallen, and how Octavian now ruled as master of land and sea. “We march not against the Jews,” he declared, “but against fugitives sons of a fallen house, who stir up the multitude. They are wolves in the fold, and it is our task to root them out before their madness spreads.” Thus encouraged, the army prepared to march south towards Galilee.

PREFACE​ Paul of Tarsus ​ I, Paul of Tarsus , though aged and near the end of life, have gathered from many sources the memory of my people, that it may not be lost in forgetfulness. The last hundred years have been the turning of an age. We might have suffered much more under Herod the Idumaean , a man cruel to the Jews and false to the Romans. His desire was always to please his Roman masters, yet he brought ruin by his tyranny. But Judea was spared the rule of his sons, who would have surpassed him in cruelty, and likewise spared the return of the Hasmoneans, who filled our past with strife and infighting. I dedicate this book to those without whom it could not be written. I give thanks to my companions Anacletus and Linus, who urged me to this task, and to Clement my disciple, whose pen surpasses mine in elegance and whose labors will endure when my own are ended. I remember Theocleia of Iconium, mother of my wife Thecla, whose piety strengthened her household. I thank Tiberius Julius Rhescuporis, king of the Bosphorans, who received me as a friend in my time of need. I give special thanks to the Emperor Gaius Caesar, princeps of Rome, protector and friend to the Jews. I also honor Agrippa, lord of Judea, though still young, from whom I received knowledge of his line and the claims of his house. Many have written of Moses our legislator, of the Judges, and of David and Solomon. Few have written of those nearer to us, though their deeds have shaped our present age. For in our own days a house has risen most unexpectedly, the Nazarenes, the family of Joseph Nazarene . After Joseph came Judas Nazarene , and from Judas came Jesus Nazarene . From them arose a dynasty unlike any before amongst the Jews, a carpenter declared King and whose descendants would be instructed in the learning of Greeks and Romans, yet holding in their breasts the hearts of Israel. They were heirs in spirit to David and Solomon, though distant in blood, and they joined the wisdom of foreigners with the faith of their fathers. I do not write to flatter Rome, for many Romans have done us wrong. Let Pompey be remembered, who defiled our Temple. Nor do I write to flatter the kings of Judea, for flattery fades and truth remains. I write that the truth may not be lost, for too many accounts are filled with falsehoods. Some magnify Rome beyond measure, others condemn our people without justice. Men have put speeches in our mouths that we never spoke, turned calamities into fables, raised up one king or cast down another according to their favor, not according to truth. Though my strength fails, I have undertaken this work, believing it useful not only to our own people but also to those among the Romans who seek the truth of their allies and their subjects. It is right that the affairs of Judea be known not by rumor or by prejudice, but as they were, in order, without addition or omission. I shall tell how a Nazarene carpenter was chosen by Rome to rule the Jews, how his sons after him bore rule, and how fortune, as with all men, preserved their line in one age and tested it in another. Let no one think that I write as an enemy of Rome, for Caesar’s authority is granted by God, nor as an enemy of our kings, for they too were appointed in their time. But I will not hide the miseries of our people, nor the errors of our rulers, nor the injustices endured, for history that flatters is not history. If at times I lament our calamities, let the reader forgive me, for I am a son of Israel, and what I write with my hand I feel also with my heart. This work I offer to Romans, to Greeks, and to barbarians alike, that all may know what came to pass. It will show how from humble beginnings a line of kings was established in Jerusalem, how a widowed carpenter was made king, how rulers were judged by their deeds, and how Rome and Judea remained joined together by providence. In these pages are not idle tales but the account of the Nazarenes, preserved for those who come after, that they may see how God raises the lowly, humbles the mighty, and directs the fate of nations.

If a carpenter from Nazareth—Jesus—had become King of the Jews in a political and historical sense, rather than being executed and later proclaimed a spiritual king by his followers, the trajectory of Jewish, Roman, and global history would likely have shifted dramatically.

First, his movement would have transformed from a marginal, apocalyptic reform movement into a political revolution within Judea. To become king, he would have needed either to defeat Roman authority or to gain recognition from it. If he had successfully led a revolt and established an independent Jewish kingdom, he might have fulfilled contemporary messianic expectations of a Davidic ruler restoring national sovereignty. In that case, his message would probably have emphasized law, governance, and national restoration more than suffering, humility, and spiritual salvation. Christianity, as it later developed around the theology of the crucifixion and resurrection, might never have emerged in the same form—or at all.

Alternatively, if Rome had installed him as a client king, his rule would likely have required compromise with imperial power. His teachings on loving enemies and rejecting violence would have faced tension with the realities of kingship—taxation, military enforcement, and political repression. The moral authority that later defined his legacy might have been diminished by the compromises of rule.

Most significantly, without crucifixion—the event that became the theological center of Christian belief—the interpretation of Jesus as a sacrificial savior may not have developed. The early Christian proclamation that his death and resurrection redeemed humanity was inseparable from his execution. A reigning king does not generate the same redemptive narrative as a crucified one. Christianity might have remained a Jewish reform sect tied to a particular kingdom, rather than evolving into a universal religion transcending ethnicity and empire.

In short, if the carpenter had become a political king, he might have changed Judean history in the short term—but it was his rejection as king and his death that enabled the rise of a global faith.

If Princess Mary Tudor—Henry VIII’s sister and the former Queen of France—had married a Bavarian prince such as Philip of Bavaria instead of Charles Brandon, the political and religious trajectory of early 16th‑century England might have shifted in subtle but meaningful ways.

First, the immediate political impact would have been diplomatic rather than domestic. Mary’s historical marriage to Charles Brandon angered Henry VIII because it was made for love and without his formal approval, but it ultimately kept her within England’s political orbit. A marriage to a Bavarian prince would have strengthened England’s ties to the Holy Roman Empire, especially the Wittelsbach dynasty, which was deeply embedded in imperial politics. Depending on timing, this could have drawn England more firmly into Habsburg-aligned continental alliances, potentially tightening relations with Emperor Charles V.

Second, such a marriage might have influenced England’s position during the early Reformation. Bavaria was a staunchly Catholic territory and later became one of the strongest centers of the Counter-Reformation. If Mary had become integrated into that dynastic network, it could have reinforced conservative Catholic alliances around Henry VIII during the 1520s and 1530s. While it is unlikely that this alone would have prevented Henry’s break with Rome—since that was driven by his marital crisis and dynastic concerns—it might have complicated his diplomatic calculations. Stronger German Catholic ties could have made isolation from Rome more costly or politically delicate.

Third, the internal English consequences could have been significant in terms of succession politics. Mary’s historical marriage to Charles Brandon produced Frances Brandon, mother of Lady Jane Grey. That lineage played a central role in the succession crisis after Edward VI’s death in 1553. If Mary had married into Bavaria instead, Lady Jane Grey would never have existed, and the attempted Protestant coup placing her on the throne would not have occurred. In that case, Mary I (Henry VIII’s daughter) might have ascended the throne with less immediate resistance, potentially stabilizing her early reign.

Finally, Mary Tudor herself would likely have remained abroad, reducing her personal influence at the English court. Her marriage to Brandon kept her close to her brother and involved in court politics. A Bavarian marriage would have removed her as a domestic political actor and tied her fate more fully to continental dynastic struggles.

In sum, while Henry VIII’s break with Rome and the broader English Reformation probably still would have occurred, a marriage between Mary Tudor and Philip of Bavaria could have strengthened Catholic diplomatic alliances, altered succession politics by eliminating the Lady Jane Grey episode, and slightly reshaped England’s continental alignments during a pivotal era.

items.question: What If All of Anne Boleyn's pregnacies came to term
human_answers: When King Henry introduced the Oath of Supremacy he made it clear that it would be treason to refuse to sign it. So he officially pardoned all seven men, telling them it was only thanks to the Queen that they were alive, but not even she would save them if he caught a whiff of them trying to stir up trouble. Many wondered what had prompted Anne to ask her husband to spare these men, after all they were all her enemies and supporters of Katherine. If all of Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had come to term and produced healthy children, the course of English and possibly European history could have been significantly different. Historically, Anne gave birth to one surviving child, Elizabeth (future Elizabeth I), and suffered several miscarriages, including at least one widely believed to have been a male fetus. The central political problem of Henry VIII’s reign—his desperate need for a legitimate male heir—might have been resolved within his second marriage.

If Anne had borne Henry a healthy son soon after Elizabeth, her position at court would have been dramatically strengthened. Much of the hostility toward her stemmed from her failure to produce a male heir. A living prince would have secured the Tudor succession, reduced factional maneuvering, and likely prevented Anne’s execution in 1536. The charges against her—adultery, incest, and treason—were almost certainly politically motivated and tied to her failure to deliver a son. With a prince in the nursery, it would have been far more difficult for Thomas Cromwell and Anne’s enemies to engineer her downfall.

A surviving son by Anne would have displaced Mary (Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon) further from the line of succession and reduced the later instability that followed Edward VI’s early death. If Anne had produced multiple surviving sons, England might not have faced the mid‑Tudor succession crises at all. Edward VI—Jane Seymour’s son—would never have been born if Anne had remained queen. Instead, Anne’s son would likely have succeeded Henry VIII directly. Depending on his health and longevity, there might have been no reigns of Mary I or Elizabeth I.

Religiously, the English Reformation may have taken a somewhat different path. Anne Boleyn was sympathetic to reformist ideas and patronized evangelical scholars. If she had remained queen for decades as the mother of the heir, reformist influence at court might have deepened earlier and perhaps more consistently. Mary I’s Catholic restoration (1553–1558) would likely never have occurred, meaning England might have avoided the Marian persecutions and the brief reconciliation with Rome. The Elizabethan Religious Settlement, as we know it, might also never have emerged, because Elizabeth herself might never have ruled.

Elizabeth I’s reign had enormous cultural and geopolitical consequences: the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flourishing of English drama, and early overseas expansion. Without Elizabeth as queen, England’s foreign policy, relations with Spain and France, and early colonial ventures could have unfolded very differently. A son of Anne might have pursued a more aggressively Protestant alliance system—or, alternatively, sought continental marriages that reshaped European power balances in new ways.

In short, if Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had all come to term, especially producing one or more healthy sons, her execution likely would not have occurred, Jane Seymour would not have become queen, and the later Tudor succession crises might have been avoided. The English Reformation would probably still have continued—since Henry had already broken with Rome—but its character, pace, and leadership would have differed substantially, and the iconic reign of Elizabeth I might never have happened.

If Elizabeth Tudor had married Robert Dudley in 1550, the consequences would have been dramatic, but the scenario depends heavily on context. In 1550, Elizabeth was still Princess Elizabeth, her half-brother Edward VI was on the throne, and Dudley was the son of John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland, one of the most powerful men in England. A marriage at that point would have been a political alliance engineered by the Dudley family to secure influence over a potential future queen.

In the short term, it would likely have strengthened the Dudley faction at court. If Elizabeth later became queen in 1558 as she did historically, Dudley would already have been her husband and thus king consort. This would have eliminated years of speculation and courtship politics that characterized her reign. However, it would also have tied her legitimacy and authority much more closely to one noble faction, undermining her careful strategy of balancing competing interests.

The marriage would have faced serious political risks. When Mary I took the throne in 1553, Elizabeth was viewed with suspicion as a Protestant heir. If she had already been married to Dudley—whose family was deeply implicated in the failed attempt to put Lady Jane Grey on the throne—Elizabeth might have been seen as even more threatening. She could have been imprisoned longer, possibly executed, or permanently sidelined. The Dudley name was closely associated with the Jane Grey coup; being married into that family might have fatally damaged Elizabeth’s position under Mary.

If both survived Mary’s reign and Elizabeth became queen with Dudley as her husband, England’s foreign and domestic politics would have shifted significantly. Elizabeth’s historical strength lay partly in remaining unmarried, which allowed her to use marriage negotiations as diplomatic leverage with France and Spain. A prior marriage would have removed that flexibility. England might have been drawn more deeply into factional struggles centered on Dudley’s ambitions. His unpopularity among some nobles could have fueled rebellion, similar to later resistance against royal favorites in other reigns.

Religiously, the Protestant settlement Elizabeth enacted would likely still have occurred, as both she and Dudley were aligned with Protestant reform. But the regime might have appeared more partisan and less moderate, potentially intensifying Catholic resistance at home and hostility abroad.

In the long term, the biggest difference would depend on whether the marriage produced children. An heir from Elizabeth and Dudley would have prevented the eventual succession of James VI of Scotland in 1603. That would have delayed or prevented the Union of the Crowns, fundamentally altering the trajectory of British state formation.

In sum, an early marriage to Robert Dudley would probably have weakened Elizabeth’s political flexibility, endangered her survival during Mary I’s reign, and reshaped the succession. It might have produced a more factional, less stable Elizabethan monarchy—and possibly a very different future for England and Scotland.

items.question: What If Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s
human_answers: Oh that's very flattering. Thank you I think the TL you're proposing is plausible and interesting re: the development of ATL Castile and Caroline War. I'm not sure the marriage with Philippa of Clarence is the way to achieve it, though. I don't share others' concerns about her inheritance, but it doesn't necessarily fit into Edward III's plans to create spheres of influence for his sons. Philippa, if she's not marrying Mortimer (who had some smaller land claims in Ireland before inheriting the Burke estates through Philippa) would seem to make more sense for a Fitzgerald or Butler or a knight of the Garter who Edward wanted to establish as a peer without alienating anything from the crown. You could argue that I am overestimating the importance of these spheres of influence. (This is around the time that Lionel gets a Visconti bride -- an arrangement negotiated to put pressure on the papacy to approve the Langley-Flanders marriage, which demonstrates that Edward III still had an overarching and interconnected dynastic plan.) But this is a period in which the Black Prince set out his own foreign policy. He does not simply rubber-stamp his father's agreements. It is TBP's decision to end the Castilian alliance when Pedro executed the prisoners from Nájera. Just a few years later, TBP vetoed his father's alliance with Charles the Bad. All of which is to ask, how would it matter to the Black Prince that his niece is queen of Castile? Or would TBP end the alliance anyway if Pedro acts the way he did in OTL? Then there is also the issue of Pedro's not-great treatment of his wives. We don't know much about Lionel (relative to his four more famous brothers), but we see Edward III and Gaunt have very close relationships with their daughters. Edward made his favorite daughter one of the greatest landholders in England and Gaunt was so fond of his eldest daughter (apparently because she reminded him of his late first wife) that he didn't marry her off until her mid 20s. If Lionel has this sort of affection for Philippa then he may not be willing to entrust his daughter to a king like Pedro. (Though, honestly, I think this is a less important point. Not only only is it entirely speculative of Lionel's personal affections, but Lionel does demonstrate a commitment to his father's plans in going through with the Visconti match for the main purpose of furthering his brother's marriage prospects in Flanders. Still, I don't thin Pedro's treatment of his wives can be entirely discounted.) I very strongly suspect that the marriage contract handed the Ulster estate over to Lionel in its entirety and entailed it to his heirs, regardless of remarriage. Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
