See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).
items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile (Pedro I, “the Cruel”) had married an English princess in the 1360s, the political map of late medieval Western Europe could have shifted significantly, especially in the context of the Hundred Years’ War and the Castilian Civil War.

In reality, Peter was allied with England through Edward of Woodstock (the Black Prince), who supported him militarily against his half-brother Henry of Trastámara. However, Peter’s legitimacy was weakened by his controversial marriage to Blanche of Bourbon (whom he abandoned) and his turbulent personal life. A formal marriage to an English princess—perhaps a daughter of Edward III—would have transformed this loose military alliance into a durable dynastic partnership.

First, it would have strengthened Peter’s claim to the Castilian throne. An English royal marriage would have enhanced his legitimacy in the eyes of European courts and possibly deterred some internal nobles from backing Henry of Trastámara. It might also have secured more sustained English military and financial support. One of the main problems Peter faced was that, after the Black Prince’s costly campaign restored him in 1367, England’s support waned. A marriage alliance could have made Castile a strategic pillar of English policy rather than a temporary intervention.

Second, it would have had major implications for the Hundred Years’ War. Historically, after Henry of Trastámara seized the throne (as Henry II), Castile became a close ally of France. The powerful Castilian fleet helped the French defeat the English at sea, most notably at the Battle of La Rochelle (1372), which was disastrous for England. If Peter had remained on the throne with English backing—and especially if he were bound by marriage—Castile’s navy would likely have supported England instead. This could have shifted naval dominance in the Channel and Bay of Biscay, improving English supply lines to Gascony and possibly prolonging or strengthening England’s position in France during the later phases of the war.

Third, dynastically, such a marriage could have created Anglo-Castilian heirs with claims to both realms. While a full political union would have been unlikely, it might have produced long-term alignment between England and Castile, potentially affecting Iberian politics for generations. The Trastámara dynasty, which later ruled not only Castile but also Aragon and influenced the eventual unification of Spain, might never have come to power—or would have done so under very different circumstances. The later marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, which united Castile and Aragon and sponsored Columbus, depended on the Trastámara line; a surviving Petrist dynasty tied to England could have altered the trajectory of Spanish state formation.

However, Peter’s own personality and governing style would still have posed problems. He alienated many Castilian nobles through harsh reprisals and centralizing tendencies. Even with English backing, internal rebellion might have continued, potentially drawing England into a prolonged and expensive Iberian conflict. If English resources were diverted heavily to Castile, this might have weakened their position in France instead of strengthening it.

In sum, an English marriage in the 1360s could have solidified Peter’s rule, prevented Castile’s alignment with France, and strengthened England’s maritime and diplomatic position in the Hundred Years’ War. The rise of the Trastámaras—and thus the later shape of Spanish unification—might have been delayed or transformed. Yet much would still have depended on Peter’s ability to reconcile his own nobility, something that even a powerful marriage alliance might not have guaranteed.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).
items.original_question: What if Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 instead of 1492 What if widespread European colonization of the Americas started 400 years earlier in 1092, the end of the 11th century? The idea I got in my head so far involves rapid advances in naval/seafaring technology to allow for trans-oceanic voyages, and the sponsor of the first voyage and colony I'm thinking would be the Duchy of Normandy, but this can change if that's not plausible enough. What I want out of the timeline spawned by the question of thread title, is a medieval retro-future colonial-frontier sort of scenario, also going by another idea-spawning question. What if the 11th century had the technology of the 15th century? What sort of tech advances, and other sorts of points of divergence, would be needed to make the beginning of European colonization of the Americans begin its proliferation in 1092 instead of 1492? And what other ideas and questions and things should I also take into consideration? My apologies for not being able to go in-depth at explaining scenarios. I'm unfortunately a very simple person with a limited education and understanding of history and other topics needed for writing alternate history. I hope to get a discussion going that will help broaden my horizons of learning more history to write better alternate history.
items.model_answer:
If sustained European colonization of the Americas had begun around 1092 instead of 1492, the trajectory of global history would have shifted dramatically—but not simply by moving the familiar Age of Exploration four centuries earlier. Medieval Europe was politically fragmented, technologically more limited, and economically less dynamic than Renaissance Europe, so the nature, pace, and consequences of colonization would likely have been very different.

First, the feasibility of sustained colonization in 1092 is uncertain. European maritime technology at the end of the 11th century was far less advanced than in the late 15th. Navigational tools like the magnetic compass were only beginning to spread in Europe, and Atlantic sailing techniques were underdeveloped outside Norse experience. The Vikings did reach North America around 1000, but they failed to establish lasting colonies partly because European states lacked the naval capacity, population surplus, and centralized financing to support transatlantic ventures. For colonization in 1092 to succeed, Europe would have needed either stronger maritime states earlier—perhaps in Scandinavia or the Iberian Peninsula—or sustained institutional backing from powerful monarchies or the Church.

If such backing had existed, colonization would likely have been slower, smaller in scale, and more decentralized. Medieval Europe had a much smaller population than in 1492, and its economy was less commercialized. Colonies might have resembled frontier outposts or crusader states rather than massive extractive empires. Feudal structures could have been transplanted across the Atlantic, producing semi-autonomous lordships owing allegiance to distant monarchs. The Church would likely have played a dominant role, framing expansion as a missionary enterprise akin to the Crusades.

The most transformative consequence would still have been epidemiological. Even in 1092, Europeans carried Old World diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza. Indigenous American populations, lacking immunity, would likely have suffered catastrophic declines, just as they did after 1492. However, because medieval Europe had a smaller population and less intense commercial integration, the demographic collapse in the Americas might have unfolded more gradually. Ironically, Europe itself would soon face the Black Death in the mid-14th century. Earlier American contact could have altered disease patterns in both directions, though it is uncertain whether major American pathogens would have significantly affected Eurasia.

Economically, Europe in 1092 was not yet positioned to exploit American silver and agricultural wealth on a massive scale. The price revolution of the 16th century, fueled by New World silver, might instead have occurred in the 12th or 13th century, potentially accelerating the decline of feudalism and the rise of monetary economies earlier. Alternatively, limited extraction capacity might have meant that American resources had a muted global impact. Crucially, earlier access to American crops—maize, potatoes, tomatoes—could have boosted European agricultural productivity centuries sooner, possibly mitigating famines and reshaping medieval demography. A more populous Europe before the Black Death might have experienced either a worse pandemic shock or a different recovery trajectory.

Global power balances would also shift. If Iberian kingdoms or Scandinavian powers had established early American footholds, they might have risen to dominance earlier. The Islamic world, then economically and scientifically more advanced than much of Europe, might have responded competitively, possibly expanding westward across the Atlantic if knowledge spread. China’s Song dynasty, technologically sophisticated and maritime-capable, might have entered transoceanic competition if aware of American lands. In this scenario, the Americas could have become a contested multipolar frontier rather than predominantly European-controlled.

Most profoundly, Indigenous American civilizations such as the Aztec and Inca empires would not have existed in their later 15th-century forms. Four centuries earlier, political configurations in Mesoamerica and the Andes were different. Earlier contact could have interrupted the rise of large centralized empires, producing entirely different patterns of alliance, resistance, and cultural exchange. Some societies might have integrated European technologies gradually rather than facing sudden conquest by gunpowder states.

In sum, colonization beginning in 1092 would likely have been slower, more feudal, and less globally transformative at first—but over time, it could have accelerated Europe’s economic and political development centuries earlier. The Columbian Exchange would still have reshaped the world, but within a medieval framework rather than a Renaissance-capitalist one. The result might have been an earlier rise of Atlantic-centered power, a restructured medieval world economy, and profoundly altered paths for both European and American civilizations.

items.question: What If Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son
human_answers: Judgement Day had finally come for Anne Boleyn. Allies and enemies, alike held their breath when the news broke that King Henry's widow was giving birth. It had been a miracle that she had managed to not miscarry on that fateful January day when her husband had fallen from his horse and would never wake up. When she had learned of Henry's death, Anne had fallen to her knees crying hysterically. However once her tears have passed and she has been calmed down, she immediately summoned the lords to form a regency council, making it clear that she will be regent, a fact that does not sit well with her uncle. Princess Elizabeth would be brought to court, both as a comfort to her mother, and in case she needed to be crowned. Lady Mary was removed from Hatfield and instead put under close guard at Hudson. The Seymours were sent away in disgrace. It was said that Queen Anne took a special delight in dismissing Jane Seymour, mocking her for ever thinking she could replace her. All of Europe held their breath as they waited to see what would happen. Not even the Pope was willing to make a move just yet, wanting to see where the land would lay. Finally on May 19, Anne went into labor. After ten grueling hours, the queen dowager finally brought her second child into the world. "Tis a healthy boy, Majesty, you have done it! You have birthed a prince!" the midwife exclaimed. "Nay, not a prince. A King. I have birthed a King!" Anne cried, a radiant smile on her face. "King Henry the Ninth!"
items.original_question: What if Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son Might make this a full TL. Not sure yet. Here is what I am wondering. Let's say that Henry dies and Anne carries her son to term. What happens? Would the people pick Mary when there is chance for a male heir? I know Norfolk and his ilk would probably not turn on Anne when there is a chance that he could be Lord Protector for fifteen years. What about Elizabeth in the meantime, would she be crowned before Anne gives birth just in case Anne gives her a sister?
items.model_answer:
If Henry VIII had died from his jousting accident in January 1536 and Anne Boleyn had subsequently given birth to a healthy son, the immediate result would have been a male Tudor heir—an infant king (effectively Henry IX)—with Anne as queen mother and central figure in the regency government.

Because the boy would have been born to a reigning king and crowned almost immediately after birth, his legitimacy under the 1534 Act of Succession (which recognized Anne’s marriage and invalidated Mary) would have been difficult to challenge legally inside England. However, his position would not have been uncontested. Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, still had strong support among conservatives and those loyal to Rome, and Emperor Charles V (her cousin) might have backed her claim diplomatically or even militarily. England could have faced serious factional tension, possibly even rebellion, centered on Mary’s cause.

Domestically, Anne would likely have headed a regency council dominated by reformist figures such as Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer. Without Henry’s later conservatism and erratic interventions, the English Reformation might have advanced more consistently in a Protestant direction during the 1530s and 1540s. The dissolution of the monasteries would almost certainly have continued, both for ideological and financial reasons. The Church of England might have adopted more explicitly reformist doctrines earlier than it did under Edward VI.

Anne herself would not have fallen in 1536, since the political crisis that destroyed her was tied to her failure to produce a living son and Henry’s desire to remarry. As queen mother to a male heir, her position would have been far stronger, though still vulnerable to factional intrigue. Her survival would also mean no marriage to Jane Seymour and no separate reign of Edward VI; the Protestant succession would be secured through Anne’s son instead.

In the long term, this scenario likely prevents the reigns of both Mary I and Elizabeth I as we know them. Mary’s path to the throne would be blocked by a legitimate male heir, and Elizabeth would remain a secondary princess unless her brother died young. If Anne’s son survived to adulthood, England would probably remain firmly Protestant without the sharp Catholic restoration under Mary or the distinctive Elizabethan religious settlement. The mid-Tudor instability of the 1540s and 1550s might have been reduced—but only if the regency weathered the dangerous early years without civil conflict over the succession.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?
items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the trajectory of the Napoleonic Wars—and much of 19th‑century Europe—would likely have changed dramatically.

By 1811 Napoleon dominated continental Europe but was locked in costly struggles: the Peninsular War in Spain and Portugal, economic warfare with Britain through the Continental System, and rising tensions with Russia. A genuine Anglo‑French peace would probably have ended the Peninsular War quickly, since British subsidies and troops were sustaining Iberian resistance. Without Wellington’s army in Portugal and Spain, Napoleon could have withdrawn hundreds of thousands of experienced troops and reduced the financial drain on France.

The most immediate consequence might have been the avoidance—or at least postponement—of Napoleon’s invasion of Russia in 1812. The Continental System existed largely to weaken Britain; if Britain were no longer at war, the rationale for forcing Russia to comply with trade restrictions would disappear. Franco‑Russian tensions would have remained, but without the economic pressure point that drove relations to collapse. Without the catastrophic Russian campaign, Napoleon would have preserved the core of his Grand Army and the aura of invincibility that had kept many European states compliant.

In Britain, peace would have eased economic strain and political unrest caused by trade disruption and war debt. British maritime and colonial dominance would likely have remained intact, since France had little ability to challenge it at sea. Britain might have focused more on imperial expansion overseas, while accepting French predominance on the continent.

For continental Europe, a stable Anglo‑French peace could have consolidated a long-lasting Napoleonic order. Client states such as the Confederation of the Rhine, the Kingdom of Italy, and the Duchy of Warsaw might have endured longer under French hegemony. Austria and Prussia, deprived of British subsidies and the opportunity created by Napoleon’s Russian disaster, would have had little immediate chance to reassert themselves. The nationalist movements in Germany and Spain might have developed more slowly without the galvanizing effect of prolonged war and French defeat.

Over the longer term, however, tensions would likely have resurfaced. Britain and France had fundamentally competing visions of European balance and global trade. Napoleon’s continental dominance and Britain’s naval and financial supremacy were structurally at odds. Even if Napoleon avoided the Russian catastrophe, managing a vast empire dependent on military power and family rule would have been difficult. Internal resistance, economic strains, and succession uncertainties would still have threatened stability.

In short, a peace in 1811 could have prevented Napoleon’s rapid downfall and prolonged French dominance in Europe, possibly delaying the restoration of monarchies and the Concert of Europe. Yet the rivalry between Britain and France, and the internal fragility of Napoleon’s system, suggest that such a peace would more likely have postponed than permanently prevented another major European conflict.

items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.
items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had concentrated its main expansion on Western Europe rather than turning toward the Levant and the Middle East, the political and cultural trajectory of Europe in the 13th century could have changed dramatically. In reality, the Mongols invaded Eastern and Central Europe in the 1240s, defeating Polish and Hungarian forces, but withdrew after the death of the Great Khan Ögedei. Had they pressed on into Germany, Italy, and France with sustained commitment and reinforcement, Western Europe—then politically fragmented and militarily decentralized—would have faced a profound crisis.

Militarily, Western European kingdoms were divided and often at odds with one another. The Holy Roman Empire was politically fractured, France was consolidating royal power but not yet dominant, and England was preoccupied with its own internal and continental struggles. The Mongols’ mobility, coordination, intelligence networks, and psychological warfare would likely have overwhelmed feudal levies and knight-based armies in open battle, just as they had done in Hungary and Poland. Major cities with strong fortifications might have resisted longer, but without coordinated continental defense, many regions could have fallen into tributary status.

Politically, a successful Mongol penetration into Western Europe might have prevented or delayed the rise of strong centralized monarchies such as Capetian France. Instead of gradual state-building, rulers may have become Mongol vassals, paying tribute in exchange for local autonomy, as happened in parts of Rus’. This could have weakened the papacy’s authority as well. The pope might have attempted to frame resistance as a crusade, but if Rome itself were threatened or subordinated, the ideological leadership of Latin Christendom would have been shaken. Alternatively, the papacy might have pursued diplomatic accommodation, as it did historically by sending envoys to the Mongols.

Economically and culturally, Mongol domination might paradoxically have increased Europe’s integration into Eurasian trade networks earlier and more deeply. Under Mongol rule, the Silk Road flourished. If Western Europe had been securely linked into this system, commercial exchange with China and Central Asia might have accelerated, potentially stimulating technological and scientific transmission earlier than in actual history. However, the destructive phase of conquest would likely have caused massive demographic and urban losses first.

Long term, much would depend on whether Mongol control endured. The Mongol Empire tended to fragment into regional khanates. A “Western Khanate” in Europe might have assimilated, intermarried, and gradually adopted Christianity, as Mongol elites elsewhere adopted Islam or Buddhism. Over generations, this could have produced hybrid ruling elites and altered aristocratic lineages across Europe. On the other hand, if Mongol rule collapsed quickly, Western Europe might have emerged more unified, forged by shared resistance, potentially accelerating political consolidation and military reform.

In short, a sustained Mongol campaign into Western Europe could have delayed or reshaped the rise of centralized monarchies, weakened papal authority, deepened Eurasian integration, and possibly altered the balance between Europe and Asia for centuries. The immediate effects would likely have been devastating, but the long-term consequences would have depended on whether Mongol power proved durable or fragmented as it did elsewhere.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If American forces had successfully captured and held Quebec in 1775–76, the province’s cultural and social development would likely have diverged sharply from the path it followed under British rule. The most important shift would have been from becoming the core of French Canadian survival within the British Empire to becoming a francophone minority region inside a new American republic.

In the short term, the Continental Congress would almost certainly have tried to honor its earlier promises to French Canadians: protection of Catholicism, continuation of French civil law, and local autonomy. Congress had already appealed to Quebec’s inhabitants in 1774–75 by criticizing Britain’s Quebec Act but also by promising representative government. To secure loyalty in wartime, the Americans likely would have allowed Catholic worship and retained elements of French civil law, at least initially. However, unlike the British Empire after 1774, the United States had no strong institutional commitment to preserving French legal and cultural autonomy over the long term.

Politically, Quebec would probably have entered the Union as one or more states, perhaps divided along the St. Lawrence valley. Early statehood would have required an elected assembly and integration into American federal structures. This would have accelerated the introduction of English-language political culture, common law influences, and Protestant Anglo-American settlers. Land tenure under the seigneurial system might have been gradually dismantled in favor of American-style private property norms, particularly as migration from New England and New York increased.

Demographically, the impact could have been transformative. Under British rule, French Canadians remained an overwhelming majority in Lower Canada well into the 19th century. Within the United States, migration pressures would likely have been far stronger. New Englanders moving north into the fertile St. Lawrence valley, combined with westward expansion routes running through the region, could have made francophones a shrinking proportion of the population by the early or mid-19th century. The cultural balance might have come to resemble Louisiana: a historically French society that retained elements of language and civil law but gradually became Anglicized and integrated into a broader American identity.

Religion would have been another key factor. The United States’ constitutional separation of church and state would have prevented the kind of formal church-state partnership that helped structure Quebec society under British rule. The Catholic Church would have remained influential locally, but without state-backed privileges or a British imperial policy designed to secure Catholic loyalty. Over time, Protestant denominations would likely have grown with Anglo-American settlement, weakening the near-monopoly the Catholic Church held in 19th-century Quebec.

National identity would also have evolved differently. In real history, French Canadian identity solidified partly in opposition to British institutions and later to Anglo-Protestant dominance within Canada. If Quebec had been American from the revolutionary era onward, its inhabitants might have developed a dual identity: culturally French but politically American, similar to how many ethnic groups in the United States retained cultural distinctiveness while embracing civic nationalism. Movements for linguistic preservation might have emerged, but probably without the same state-centered nationalism that later fueled Quebecois separatism. There would be no Confederation in 1867 to rally against, and no Canadian federal framework within which Quebec could claim founding-nation status.

Internationally, the capture of Quebec would also have altered continental geopolitics. Without a British-controlled Canada, there would have been less incentive for Loyalists to migrate north, reducing the development of an English-speaking Ontario as a counterweight to French Quebec. The entire northern tier of North America might have become American much earlier, further embedding Quebec within a predominantly English-speaking republic.

Overall, Quebec under American control would likely have experienced stronger demographic and linguistic assimilation pressures. French language and civil law traditions might have survived regionally—especially if protected early on—but the long-term trajectory would probably resemble partial integration rather than the sustained, institutionally supported distinct society that developed within Canada. Quebec would still be culturally marked by its French origins, but it would be far less politically and nationally distinct than it became in Canadian history.

items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies
items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence—meaning the American Revolution either failed or never occurred—the British colonies in North America would likely have remained within the British Empire and evolved along lines similar to Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

In the short term, Britain would have continued tightening imperial administration after the Seven Years’ War. The imperial reforms that sparked colonial resistance—taxation measures, trade regulation, and stronger royal oversight—would likely have been implemented more gradually or negotiated into a more federated imperial system. London may have granted the colonies greater parliamentary representation or expanded colonial self-government to prevent unrest, much as it later did in white settler colonies.

Over the nineteenth century, British North America would probably have consolidated into one or more large self-governing dominions. The Thirteen Colonies might have been reorganized alongside Canada into a federated “Dominion of North America,” with responsible government, a local parliament, and autonomy over domestic affairs while foreign policy and defense remained under British control. This mirrors the path Canada followed after 1867.

Westward expansion would likely still have occurred, but under tighter imperial management. British policy before 1776 aimed to regulate settlement beyond the Appalachians to stabilize relations with Indigenous nations. Without U.S. independence and its aggressive land speculation and expansionist ideology, westward growth may have been slower, more centralized, and more treaty-based—though still ultimately expansionist, as seen in Canada and Australia.

Slavery would probably have been abolished earlier than it was in the United States. The British Empire abolished slavery in 1833. In a British North America that included the southern colonies, slavery might have ended at that time across the continent, potentially avoiding a civil war like the American Civil War. However, this would have required managing strong planter resistance, particularly in colonies such as Virginia and South Carolina.

Politically, the region would likely have evolved into a parliamentary system under a constitutional monarchy rather than a presidential republic. There would be no U.S. Constitution as we know it; instead, governance would follow the Westminster model with a prime minister, cabinet government, and a governor-general representing the Crown.

Globally, the absence of an independent United States would have significantly altered power balances. Britain might have remained the dominant North Atlantic power longer, supported by a vast and unified North American dominion. The French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars would still have occurred, but without a U.S. republic as a political model. In the twentieth century, a British-led North America would likely have entered world wars as part of the Empire/Commonwealth, similar to Canada but on a much larger scale.

In summary, if the United States had never existed, British North America would most plausibly have developed into one or more large self-governing dominions within the British Empire—politically similar to Canada but territorially vast—featuring parliamentary government, earlier empire-wide abolition of slavery, more gradual constitutional evolution, and continued cultural and institutional ties to Britain.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. This is what I have in mind: 1.
