If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505 instead of becoming Henry VIII’s queen, the political and religious trajectory of England—and to a lesser extent Italy and Spain—would likely have changed profoundly.

In 1505 Catherine was still technically the widow of Arthur, Prince of Wales, and her future in England was uncertain. A marriage to Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria (the heir to the dispossessed Neapolitan royal house of Aragon), would have kept her firmly within the orbit of Spanish dynastic politics rather than English ones. This would have strengthened Aragonese claims in southern Italy and possibly reinforced Spanish influence in Naples during the ongoing Italian Wars. Catherine, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, would have been a prestigious match, bolstering the duke’s legitimacy and perhaps positioning Naples more securely within the Spanish imperial system rather than as a contested territory between France and Spain.

For England, the consequences would have been dramatic. Henry VIII would not have married Catherine in 1509. Without that marriage, there would have been no prolonged struggle over the lack of a surviving male heir, and thus no “Great Matter”—Henry’s campaign to annul his marriage on the grounds of biblical prohibition. The English Reformation, at least in its initial form, was driven by Henry’s desire to remarry and secure a male successor. If Catherine had never been his wife, there would have been no need to seek a papal annulment and no immediate trigger for the break with Rome in the 1530s.

This does not mean England would have remained permanently Catholic. Protestant ideas were already spreading in Europe, and reformist currents existed within England. However, without royal sponsorship, reform would likely have proceeded more slowly and perhaps along lines similar to those in Spain or Italy—internal Catholic reform rather than schism. The Church of England as a separate national church might never have emerged, or it might have arisen later under different circumstances.

Dynastically, Henry would have needed another bride. He might have married into the French royal family, a German princely house, or another Iberian line. A French marriage, for instance, could have shifted England’s alliances during the Italian Wars, potentially aligning England more closely with France against the Habsburgs. Alternatively, a Habsburg match could have tied England more tightly to the emerging empire of Charles V. The specific choice would have significantly shaped European power politics in the early sixteenth century.

Mary I of England would never have been born, eliminating the later Marian restoration of Catholicism. Likewise, Elizabeth I—daughter of Anne Boleyn—would not have existed in her historical form, since Anne’s rise depended on Henry’s desire to replace Catherine. Without Elizabeth, England’s later religious settlement, naval expansion, and cultural “Elizabethan” flowering would have taken a different shape, perhaps under a Tudor son by another queen or under a different dynasty if the succession faltered.

In Naples, Catherine as duchess (and potentially queen, depending on how events unfolded) would have brought formidable political skill and dynastic prestige. She was well educated, devout, and experienced in governance. Her presence might have strengthened Aragonese-Spanish authority in southern Italy, but Naples’ fate would still largely depend on the broader Habsburg-Valois struggle. Given Spain’s eventual dominance in Italy under Charles V, Catherine’s marriage could have symbolized and reinforced that consolidation.

In sum, Catherine marrying Ferdinand of Calabria in 1505 would likely have prevented the immediate cause of England’s break with Rome, reshaped Tudor succession, and altered the diplomatic alignments of early sixteenth-century Europe. The English Reformation as we know it—rooted in Henry VIII’s marital crisis—might never have occurred, or would have emerged later and in a very different form.

items.question: What If Dynamite Invented During the Renaissance?
human_answers: I was also wondering how this would affect Venice’s canals but I just realized they’re currently going through the Italian Wars… my idea is 1450: Some guy in London blows himself up mixing soap with aqua fortis and oil of vitriol. Thomas Norton records this in his books on alchemy and knowledge of “aqua ignis” is published. 1470: The War of Roses reaches its peak, Tudors and Lancastrians flee to France and while Yorkists flee to Flanders. These exiled nobles hire alchemists find ways using "aqua ignis” in warfare but their resources are too few and the substance is too difficult to be produced. The formula becomes widespread across the continent and beyond. 1490: King Charles VIII of France commissions “flasks of aqua ignis” to be used in his invasion of Italy alongside the newly invented arquebus. Aqua ignis however is incredibly unstable and soldiers are unable to transport the substance without blowing themselves up. The French effort is widely considered a failure, but his ideas are noted by the Venetians as they go to war with the Pope. 1500: Alchemists in Venice (maybe a little da Vinci cameo but he was hardly an alchemist) start experimenting on ignium and make some interesting observations. They discover that “aqua ignis” stabilizes when mixed with wood pulp and chalk, creating the formula for dynamite which becomes known as “ignium”. However, alchemists fail to produce enough oil of vitriol to make mass produced ignuim viable in warfare. 1540: Paracelcus, the Swiss German alchemist, discovers Joshua Ward’s method for creating sulfuric acid around 200 years early. When mixing sulfur and saltpeter inside giant glass wars with a bit of water, the vapor condenses into oil of vitriol. He dies soon after from mercury poisoning, but the Holy Roman Emperor makes note of his discovery. 1550: The last of the Italian Wars begin. Swiss pike squares, French gunmen, and Ottoman raiders are blown to bits by barrels of ignium catapulted across the battlefield. The Hapsburgs eagerly adopt this new weapon, setting up new factories to mass produce ignium in Germany and Iberia. Meanwhile, alchemists and dissenting thinkers fleeing the counter reformation bring these methods of production to the Emperor’s enemies. Christendom is split in two, a new world is discovered, and the face of warfare is changed forever by this new invention.
items.original_question: What if Dynamite Invented During the Renaissance? Dynamite in our world was invented in 1867 by Alfred Noble as a way to stabilize nitroglycerin, an explosive mix of nitric and sulfuric acids with glycerol (the main ingredient in fat-based soap), by mixing it with clay and chalk. Nitroglycerin, however was only discovered 20 years before Noble’s invention earned him the Noble Prize. But what if things were different? Aqua fortis (nitric acid) and oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) both existed in medieval Europe and were used by OTL alchemists to dissolve gold for their experiments. Maybe an alchemist tries perfecting the ingredient to turn lead into gold but spills his formula all over his workbench. And when he tries to clean up it up with a soapy rag, he blows himself up, leaving his apprentice to record this newfound discovery. In any case, the year is 1450 and King Henry VI’s “alchemy craze” has taken England by storm. In this craze, nitroglycerin is discovered. Maybe it takes several more decades, if not a century, before alchemists learn how to turn this strange concoction into dynamite. What next?
items.model_answer:
If dynamite had been invented during the Renaissance—say in the 15th or 16th century—it would likely have accelerated several major transformations already underway in Europe and beyond.

Militarily, the Renaissance was an era of rapid change driven by gunpowder weapons, cannons, and fortified cities designed to withstand artillery. Dynamite, being far more powerful and portable than black powder, would have dramatically increased the destructive capability of armies and navies. Siege warfare would have shifted quickly: fortified walls, even the advanced star forts designed to resist cannon fire, might have become obsolete much sooner. This could have centralized power faster in emerging nation-states, since rulers with access to dynamite could crush rebellious cities and rival nobles more decisively. At the same time, the scale of battlefield destruction would likely have intensified, potentially making wars shorter but more devastating.

In exploration and empire-building, dynamite would have made mining and infrastructure projects far easier. Renaissance Europe was entering the age of global exploration and colonial expansion. Easier excavation of minerals—especially silver and gold in the Americas—could have accelerated the flow of wealth into Europe, strengthening imperial powers like Spain and Portugal earlier and more dramatically. Road-building, canal construction, and harbor development would also have advanced more quickly, possibly speeding up economic integration and trade networks.

Architecturally and scientifically, the Renaissance was marked by ambitious engineering projects—cathedrals, domes, canals, and early scientific experimentation. Dynamite could have enabled more daring construction, tunneling, and quarrying, potentially advancing civil engineering by centuries. However, the scientific understanding of chemistry at the time was limited. Without modern safety protocols and materials science, dynamite production would likely have been unstable and extremely dangerous. Accidental explosions in dense urban centers could have been frequent and catastrophic.

Politically and socially, access to such a powerful explosive might have destabilized societies. Renaissance Europe was already rife with religious conflict and peasant uprisings. Dynamite in the hands of rebels, mercenaries, or assassins could have amplified political violence. The Reformation and subsequent religious wars might have become even more destructive, possibly leading to harsher state surveillance and control earlier in history.

Globally, if European powers possessed dynamite during early encounters with the Americas, Africa, and Asia, the imbalance of military power could have been even more extreme. Conquests might have occurred faster and with greater devastation, reshaping demographic and cultural histories even more dramatically.

Overall, dynamite in the Renaissance would likely have accelerated state centralization, imperial expansion, military transformation, and large-scale engineering—while also increasing the destructiveness of war and political conflict. It would not have changed the direction of history entirely, but it could have compressed centuries of technological and political development into a much shorter, more violent span.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini
items.model_answer:
The phrase “Seven Bishops’ Death in 1558” does not correspond to a well-known historical event. However, 1558 was a pivotal year in English history because it marked the death of Queen Mary I and the accession of Elizabeth I. If the question is asking what might have happened if a major cluster of episcopal deaths had not occurred in 1558—or, more broadly, if the episcopal leadership of the English Church had remained stable at that moment—the consequences would likely have centered on the English Reformation and Elizabeth’s religious settlement.

When Elizabeth I came to the throne in November 1558, the English episcopate was overwhelmingly Catholic, appointed under Mary I. Elizabeth’s Protestant Religious Settlement of 1559 depended in part on replacing resistant Catholic bishops with clergy willing to accept royal supremacy and moderate Protestant reforms. In reality, many Marian bishops refused to take the Oath of Supremacy and were deprived of their sees, allowing Elizabeth to appoint reform-minded successors.

If those bishops had not died or been removed—if, for example, they had remained in office and successfully resisted deprivation—the Elizabethan Religious Settlement would have faced far greater institutional resistance. Parliament might still have passed the Act of Supremacy and Act of Uniformity, but enforcing them would have been much harder without compliant bishops to ordain clergy, administer dioceses, and implement liturgical change. The Church of England might have evolved more slowly, perhaps retaining more Catholic forms or facing deeper internal conflict.

Alternatively, if a hypothetical event involving seven prominent bishops had strengthened Catholic leadership in 1558, it could have bolstered resistance to Elizabeth’s reforms and possibly encouraged foreign Catholic powers, such as Spain or the Papacy, to intervene more aggressively in English affairs. This might have intensified religious polarization earlier than occurred historically.

In short, without a disruption in episcopal leadership around 1558, Elizabeth’s religious settlement would likely have been more difficult to impose, potentially resulting in a more contested, unstable, or even more overtly Catholic-leaning English Church in the early years of her reign.

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. If Sulla had gone east to fight Mithridates VI as he historically did, but Marius had been the one to march on Rome first, the late Republic’s political trajectory could have shifted in tone and legacy—though probably not in ultimate outcome. The core structural crisis of the Republic would have remained.

Historically, Sulla’s unprecedented march on Rome in 88 BCE shattered the taboo against using Roman legions against the city itself. That act normalized civil war as a political instrument. If, instead, Marius had marched first to secure the Mithridatic command after the Assembly transferred it to him, the symbolic weight of initiating civil war would have fallen on him and the populares faction rather than on Sulla and the optimates.

Marius, unlike Sulla, did not possess the same aristocratic ideological commitment to restoring senatorial supremacy. His earlier career had been built on popular support, military reform, and rivalry with the Senate’s conservative elite. If he had marched on Rome, he likely would have framed the action as defending the sovereignty of the popular assemblies against senatorial obstruction. However, once a Roman general used his army to settle a political dispute in the city, the constitutional damage would have been identical. The Rubicon would have been crossed two generations earlier.

Sulla, in this scenario, campaigning successfully against Mithridates in the East, would have gained immense prestige, wealth, and loyal veteran legions—just as he did historically. Upon returning to Italy, he would have confronted a Marian regime that had already violated constitutional norms by military force. The moral high ground Sulla claimed in reality—avenging an illegal seizure of command—would be even stronger. He could plausibly present himself as restoring order after Marius’ armed demagoguery.

The likely result is still civil war in Italy, but with roles rhetorically reversed. Sulla might still have won, given his military competence and eastern resources. If victorious, he may have imposed reforms similar to his historical dictatorship: strengthening the Senate, curbing tribunes, restructuring courts, and settling veterans on confiscated land. However, his proscriptions might have been framed more explicitly as punishment for the first violators of the sacred pomerium—Marius and his supporters.

Alternatively, if Marius had consolidated power more effectively—perhaps avoiding the instability and factionalism that plagued his historical seventh consulship—he might have preempted Sulla’s return by raising additional forces and purging Sullan sympathizers more thoroughly. In that case, Rome might have experienced a Marian authoritarian settlement instead of a Sullan one: increased empowerment of the tribunate, deeper integration of Italian allies, and possibly a more enduring populares dominance. Yet Marius was elderly and in poor health by 88–87 BCE; his death shortly thereafter was likely in any timeline, leaving leadership to figures like Cinna. That suggests instability would still follow.

In the broader sweep, the Republic’s underlying problems—personal armies loyal to generals, massive inequality, provincial wealth, and competition for extraordinary commands—would remain unresolved. Whether the first marcher was Sulla or Marius, the precedent of armed intervention in politics would be set. The careers of Pompey, Crassus, and eventually Caesar would still unfold in a political culture accustomed to military strongmen.

The main difference, then, would be narrative legitimacy and factional memory. Sulla would not be remembered as the first man to turn legions on Rome; Marius would. The ideological stain would attach to the populares rather than the optimates. But the structural decay of republican norms—and the eventual rise of one-man rule—would likely still occur. The Republic was already too militarized and too competitive at the top for a single reversal of roles to save it.

items.original_question: What if al-Andalus survives The 11th century was a pivotal moment in Hispanic history. At the beginning of the century, the Caliphate of Córdoba was the dominant power on the peninsula. The city of Córdoba rivaled Constantinople as the largest city in Europe. Ostensibly ruled by the Umayyads under Caliph Hisham II, in reality he was merely a puppet of his ambitious hajib (chamberlain) Abu Amir Muhammad ‘ al-Mansur ’ more famously known as Almanzor. A highly ambitious man, Almanzor would import thousands of Berber tribesmen into al-Andalus to serve in Córdoba’s army. He would utilize this army to not only keep the disgruntled Arab elites in line but also to bring the Christian north to heel through large-scale annual raids. While this arrangement put strain on the treasury and created ethnic strife, it was effective, and upon his death in 1002 AD Almanzor would be seamlessly succeeded by his son al-Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar would continue his father’s regime, continuing to import Berbers, continuing to raid the north, and keeping the state stable. It was looking like a dual-power dynamic was emerging in Córdoba just as it had back east in Baghdad. However, while on campaign against Castile, al-Muzaffar would die unexpectedly in 1008 AD. His younger brother Sanchuelo would succeed him as hajib , but he would lack the brilliance of his father or the prudence of his brother. Sanchuelo would offend the Arab nobility by having Hisham II name him as his heir as Caliph. This act would trigger the Fitna of al-Andalus, reducing the grand city of Córdoba to ruins and shattering the country into 30+ squabbling petty kingdoms or taifas. Suddenly, the power dynamic was reversed. Now the Muslim south was paying tribute to the Christian north. The north would consolidate under the Jiménez dynasty, and then push south, culminating in the capture of Toledo in 1085 AD, followed by the occupation of the rest of al-Andalus by the Berber Almoravid dynasty from Morocco. The rest of the Reconquista would unfold in the following centuries. The Fitna proved to be a lucky break for Christian Iberia, as without the might of Córdoba crushing them, the Reconquista started to truly gain steam. However, what if the Fitna was averted or delayed by having al-Muzaffar not die prematurely in 1008? Had he not died young, Sanchuelo likely never comes to power. This alone averts the triggering of the Fitna . Of course, the underlying financial issues and ethnic strife still exist, so the Fitna may still occur under different circumstances. However it’s likely to be nowhere as devestating for al-Andalus as IOTL. How would a continuing Caliphate of Córdoba navigate the rest of the 11th century? Would al-Andalus remain powerful and prosperous as we transition into the High Middle Ages? Could the Andalusi withstand pressure from both Christians and Berbers alike? Will the Reconquista ever happen without al-Andalus collapsing?
items.model_answer:
If al-Andalus had survived as a durable Muslim polity in Iberia—whether as a unified caliphate, a stable federation of taifas, or a kingdom resilient against Christian expansion—the political, cultural, and global trajectory of Europe and the Mediterranean would likely have been significantly altered.

Politically, the Reconquista would have stalled or taken a very different form. A stable al-Andalus could have maintained a balance of power with the Christian kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, and Portugal, perhaps resulting in a permanently divided Iberian Peninsula, similar to the coexistence of Christian and Muslim polities in the eastern Mediterranean. The eventual unification of Spain under Ferdinand and Isabella might never have occurred, or would have emerged as a smaller Christian state without control over all Iberia. This in turn could have delayed or reshaped overseas expansion, since the Spanish monarchy’s consolidation of power and resources—crucial for funding Columbus in 1492—was tied directly to the conquest of Granada. Without a unified Spain at that moment, the early phases of Atlantic empire-building might have been led more decisively by Portugal, France, or even an Andalusi state.

Culturally and intellectually, a surviving al-Andalus would likely have remained a major center of scholarship, science, and interreligious exchange. Medieval al-Andalus was already a conduit for transmitting classical Greek knowledge, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy into Latin Christendom. If this environment had endured, Europe might have experienced a longer and more continuous period of cross-cultural fertilization. Jewish communities, which flourished at times under Muslim rule and later faced expulsion from Christian Spain in 1492, might have retained a stable intellectual homeland in Iberia. The expulsions of Jews and Muslims from Spain might not have occurred at all, altering the demographic and economic development of both Iberia and the Ottoman Empire, which absorbed many Sephardic Jews.

Religiously, the continued presence of a powerful Muslim state in western Europe would have complicated the narrative of a uniformly Christian Europe. The Protestant Reformation and Catholic Counter-Reformation might have unfolded differently if a significant Islamic power existed just beyond (or within) the boundaries of Christendom. The concept of European identity itself—often defined in contrast to Islam after the Middle Ages—might have been more pluralistic or more sharply polarized, depending on the nature of Andalusi-Christian relations.

Economically, al-Andalus could have served as a permanent bridge between the Islamic world, Africa, and Europe. Its survival might have strengthened Mediterranean trade networks relative to Atlantic ones, potentially slowing the shift of economic gravity toward northern Europe. Alternatively, an outward-looking Andalusi state might have participated in Atlantic exploration, bringing Islamic navigational science and commercial networks into early transoceanic expansion.

Globally, the colonization of the Americas would likely have been different in language, religion, and governance. Without a unified Catholic Spain, the religious character of Latin America might have been more diverse, and the geopolitical competition over the New World more fragmented from the outset. A Muslim Iberian power might even have competed for Atlantic territories, introducing Islamic political and legal traditions into parts of the Americas.

In sum, the survival of al-Andalus would not simply have preserved a medieval Muslim kingdom in Iberia; it would have reshaped the formation of Spain, the course of European state-building, the dynamics of religious identity, and possibly the pattern of global exploration and empire. The most profound change might have been a Europe whose political and cultural boundaries were less rigidly defined by a Christian–Muslim divide, and whose early modern development emerged from a more visibly pluralistic foundation.

If Louis the Pious had successfully implemented his reforms and secured a stable, uncontested succession, the Carolingian Empire might have remained politically unified for a longer period, significantly altering the trajectory of medieval Europe.

Louis aimed to preserve imperial unity through the Ordinatio Imperii (817), which sought to establish a clear hierarchical inheritance system under his eldest son Lothar while granting sub-kingdoms to his younger sons. His failure stemmed largely from repeated revisions to succession plans, aristocratic factionalism, and civil wars among his heirs. If he had managed to enforce a stable succession—perhaps by preventing repeated partitions and suppressing noble revolts—the empire might not have fractured in 843 under the Treaty of Verdun.

A continued unified Carolingian Empire would likely have delayed or prevented the emergence of distinct political entities that later became France and Germany. Without Verdun’s division into West, Middle, and East Francia, linguistic and political divergence might have developed more slowly. A stronger central authority could also have resisted Viking, Magyar, and Saracen incursions more effectively, reducing the degree of feudal decentralization that characterized the 9th and 10th centuries.

Moreover, a stable imperial structure might have reinforced the idea of a continuous Western Roman-style empire in Western Europe centuries before the Ottonians revived the imperial title in East Francia. The papacy’s political role might have evolved differently as well, since papal reliance on regional rulers would have been less necessary under a powerful, unified Carolingian monarchy.

That said, structural pressures—geographic vastness, weak communications, and aristocratic autonomy—would still have posed long-term challenges. Even with successful reforms, decentralization may have eventually emerged. However, European political boundaries, the development of France and Germany, and the balance of power in the early Middle Ages would likely have looked markedly different, with a stronger, longer-lasting Carolingian imperial core shaping the continent’s development.

Consequently, Japan’s expansionist trajectory once again focused on the Korean Peninsula, Manchuria, and the Asian continent. What I am curious about is the following. If Japan were to become a country in which the navy held complete primacy over the army, how would its history have needed to unfold differently? In this scenario, the army would be limited to roles such as suppression of internal rebellions, defense of the home islands, and naval infantry (marines), possessing only minimal status and political influence. The navy would constitute the principal military force, and national defense strategy and institutional design would likewise be shaped under naval leadership. Furthermore, the direction of external expansion would be determined from the perspective of a maritime power, rather than that of a continental state. If Japan had chosen the route of a maritime power like Britain or the Venetian Republic, or if its modernization had been deliberately oriented toward a completely navy-led military structure, how would Japanese history have unfolded differently? The Japan I'm referring to includes not only the Empire of Japan but also earlier periods of Japanese history. POD is not just in 1868 but extends to several centuries earlier.
items.model_answer:
If Japan had pursued a consistently navy-centered national strategy—prioritizing maritime power over continental expansion—the trajectory of its modern history could have been markedly different.

Historically, Japan oscillated between two strategic visions after the Meiji Restoration: a “strike north” strategy focused on continental expansion into Korea, Manchuria, and China (favored by the Army), and a “strike south” or maritime strategy centered on naval dominance and sea-lane control (favored by the Navy). In reality, interservice rivalry and the growing influence of the Army pushed Japan toward continental entanglements that culminated in the Sino-Japanese War (1937) and eventually war with the United States.

A genuinely navy-centered strategy would likely have emphasized maritime commerce, colonial consolidation, and sea control over large-scale land conquest. Japan might have focused on securing and developing Taiwan, Korea, and possibly limited Pacific island holdings, while avoiding deep military involvement in mainland China. Naval leaders generally understood that Japan lacked the industrial capacity to defeat the United States in a prolonged war, so a navy-dominant government may have been more cautious about provoking Washington. Maintaining access to American oil and trade would have been a strategic priority, reducing the incentive for the southward push that triggered the Pacific War.

Such a strategy could have pushed Japan toward something closer to a British-style maritime empire: commercially driven, naval-protected, and dependent on stable sea lanes rather than territorial annexation of vast continental spaces. Economic integration with Southeast Asia might have been pursued through trade and influence rather than outright invasion. Without the quagmire in China and the embargoes that followed, Japan’s industrial growth may have been steadier and less distorted by total war mobilization.

However, this path would not have guaranteed peace. A navy-centered Japan would still have sought regional dominance in East Asia and the western Pacific. Competition with the United States and Britain over influence in China and Southeast Asia might still have intensified. Yet conflict might have taken the form of naval arms races, diplomatic crises, and limited confrontations rather than full-scale total war. The Washington Naval Treaty system, instead of collapsing, might have been extended or renegotiated as a framework for managed rivalry.

Domestically, a navy-led strategy might also have moderated the rise of radical ultranationalism tied to Army factions. The Army’s culture of continental expansion, mass mobilization, and ideological warfare was central to the brutality in China. A maritime orientation could have fostered a more technocratic and commercially oriented elite, potentially limiting the extreme militarization of society in the 1930s.

In the most optimistic version of this counterfactual, Japan becomes a dominant maritime-industrial power integrated into global trade, avoiding catastrophic war with the United States and the atomic bombings. In a less optimistic version, it still collides with American power but from a stronger economic and diplomatic position, perhaps producing a shorter or more limited conflict.

Overall, a navy-centered national strategy would likely have reduced Japan’s commitment to continental conquest, reshaped its domestic politics, and significantly altered the path to World War II—possibly averting the Pacific War as it unfolded, though not necessarily eliminating great-power rivalry in East Asia.

items.question: What If Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829?
human_answers: The Know-Nothings don't exist yet in the 1820s. That said, there is something that might alienate him from the nascent Whigs - he's a Freemason, and a pretty involved one - he was Grand Master of the Grand Orient of France during Napoleon's entire reign as emperor, founded the National Lodge of Spain, and that aspect in particular helped hurt his legitimacy among the Spanish when he was made king there. Now, the period where Joseph would enter American politics in your scenario largely coincides with the spread of the Anti-Masonic movement in New York, and their members would largely go on to integrate the Whig party later down the line. In the other hand, as time passed, the Anti-Masonic aspect was diluted so much that they ended up running a Mason as their 1832 presidential candidate, who even defended the Order in a speech before the convention that nominated him, so he might go either way.

In 1908? Highly doubtful, given Bonaparte's Catholic faith. That wouldn't have played at all in much of the South (not that it would have mattered much in terms of getting votes for the GOP there), and might have been a hindrance elsewhere. If he had somehow gotten the nomination, his running mate would certainly have been a Protestant from (likely) the midwest (Albert Beveridge?); TR would have had to do some strenuous campaigning on his behalf especially if Bryan (often referred to as "the Protestant pope") had been his opponent. The result would have been close if Bonaparte had won, and he'd have had to go to great lengths to demonstrate his independence from the Vatican. Still, the idea is intriguing: imagine the polling place schizophrenia of the Irish community in Boston, for example, given how accustomed that segment was to voting a straight Democrat ticket at the time. Also fascinating: Bonaparte was a strong advocate for civil rights for African-Americans. Had he somehow been elected, perhaps the entire cause of civil rights might have been advanced five years or so.
items.original_question: What if Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829? Joseph Bonaparte in the early 1830s. ​ Yes, this is completely unrealistic, but it's not quite as outlandish as an actual ASB (hence why I'm posting it on here), as it was theoretically something that could have happened. Joseph Bonaparte had lived in the US since 1817, seemed to have been relatively well-liked during his time in America, and to be a senator you need to be a US citizen for at least nine years. Theoretically, had the former king of Naples and then Spain had desired it, he could have very well becoming a senator by the beginning of the Jacksonian period, when both of New Jersey's seats in the US senate were up for grabs in the 1828-29 senate elections. For this scenario, Joseph Bonaparte comes to decide he wants to integrate himself in the United States. After becoming a US citizen in 1819, Joseph manages to be elected to the US Senate representing New Jersey in the 1828-29. replacing Theodore Frelinghuysen from our own timeline. What exactly happens, domestically, and in terms of the US' relationships with foreign countries, and in any other conceivable aspect, in this timeline where a former monarch manages to become a US Senator at the beginning of the Jackson administration.
items.model_answer:
If Joseph Bonaparte had become a U.S. senator in 1829, it would have been politically dramatic but structurally limited in impact. By that time, he had been living in New Jersey for over a decade, cultivating elite American contacts while remaining a symbol of European monarchy. His election would have depended on a state legislature (senators were chosen by legislatures until 1913) willing to elevate a former King of Spain and Naples—something controversial in a republic deeply sensitive to aristocratic influence.

In the short term, his presence would have fueled partisan debate. Jacksonian Democrats were rising in 1829, emphasizing popular sovereignty and suspicion of entrenched elites. Joseph, a European aristocrat with Napoleonic associations, would likely have been attacked as a symbol of Old World corruption. The National Republicans (and later Whigs) might have found him more compatible, especially if he supported internal improvements, a national bank, or protective tariffs. However, his foreign birth would have constrained him politically: although naturalized citizens could serve in the Senate after nine years of citizenship, public suspicion of foreign influence would have limited his credibility.

On foreign policy, he might have played a modest advisory role. His knowledge of European courts and Napoleonic diplomacy could have informed debates over relations with France, Spain, and Latin America. During the era of the Monroe Doctrine and expanding U.S. trade, a senator with firsthand European experience might have encouraged stronger commercial and diplomatic ties, particularly with post-Napoleonic France. Still, U.S. foreign policy in the 1830s was driven more by expansionism and hemispheric concerns than by European dynastic politics, so his influence would likely have been consultative rather than transformative.

Domestically, his impact would probably have been symbolic rather than legislative. He was not deeply embedded in American party machinery, and without a strong regional base beyond elite circles in New Jersey and Philadelphia, he would have struggled to command broad coalitions. He may have supported infrastructure and cultural institutions—reflecting his Enlightenment leanings—but he would not likely have altered the trajectory of major issues such as Indian removal, nullification, or the Bank War, which were shaped by powerful American political figures and sectional forces.

The most lasting effect might have been cultural and psychological. A former European king serving as a U.S. senator would have reinforced the American narrative that the republic could absorb and repurpose Old World elites under constitutional norms. It would have underscored the permeability between European upheaval and American political life in the early nineteenth century. Yet the institutional structure and partisan dynamics of the era suggest that Joseph Bonaparte’s Senate career would have been more notable for symbolism and curiosity than for reshaping American history.

items.question: What If Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg?
human_answers: I mean, that was more or less the agreement. France would likely gain the Austrian Netherlands unless Austria withdrew from the deal. However, I'm not sure if they would do that. What, Germany? The kingdom that united the German kingdoms is no longer a great power. France, which became a republic in OTL, may very well not experience total collapse, instead becoming a constitutional monarchy. Eliminating the entire process of potentially creating Germany. Honestly, the idea of Germany may very well never leave the drawing board. Austria didn't really want to unify the German kingdoms; it was quite happy with the kingdoms being linked to it but not absorbed. Perhaps some form of federation of northern Germany will occur, but that's not a certainty.

Then I think you really have to run through the events of the 1770-80s to figure out what the international scene looks like by the 1790s which in tern dictates how much room to maneuver Austria has in Germany as the subject of Imperial reform becomes a pressing issue. I still think the Greek Plan is a fantasy but its entirely possible that Austria recovers something along the lines of the Passarowitz borders, perhaps incrementally over the course or the rest of the century. ITTL attention Austria will be focused squarely to the south and the Danube so gains in Serbia, Bosnia and Wallachia are likely but Moldavia less so. Poland meanwhile probably does not undergo partition and remains a Russian client state in the near term. Although its also possible in a different context post ATL Seven Years War that the Polish Royal election in 1764 leads to a falling out between Russia and Austria. Then the next big question is whether the French revolution still breaks out and still proceeds as IOTL and what kind of state Austria is in internally at the end of Joseph II's reign. Presumably even if the Josephine reforms spark a backlash Austria is much better positioned to ride them out with the southern border secure and gains already made from the Ottomans and with no Prussia threat in the north. So even if the Austrian Netherlands break out in rebellion Joseph or Leopold would be able to put down the revolt more easily without it posing any kind of existential threat.

Considering that theoretically the agreement signed between Russia, Austria and Saxony, envisaged a territorial exchange between Royal Prussia and Courland ( with the recognition that the Wettins would retain the throne of the PLC ) while the Habsburgs would recover Silesia or parts of it, that said, the internal balance of the HRE, would be brought back to the previous Leopoldine period, with Vienna as the undisputed leader, and therefore there would be more room for maneuver to try to pass a new package of imperial reforms, certainly France gaining control of the Austrian Netherlands, would not let the imperial princes of the Rhineland and the Hanoverians sleep peacefully, but unfortunately the latter pay the price of having sided with Prussia or of wanting to remain neutral, regarding the possible idea of German unification, it is difficult for the Habsburgs to show a real interest, when they would prefer to maintain the Status Quo or at most consolidate their position in Swabia / Bavaria ( I could see the Bavarian crisis being easily resolved through an agreement, with Charles Theodore inheriting a good part of the duchy, while Vienna annexes small border areas ) finally I am of the opinion that in this scenario, the role of leadership of the Protestant front ( in Otl led by Berlin ) will be taken by the Hanover, who paradoxically will have to review their political priorities ( especially from the London point of view ), because with their choices they will find themselves diplomatically isolated, therefore they will necessarily have to be more active on the continent

It was already happening: Elizabeth could not force Buturlin to get out of his bases and start acting against Prussia. The only meaningful operation was capture of Kolberg and even it was to provide a secure supply line because the Austrians were refusing to do so and getting supplies from the PLC was extremely problematic. Among the Russian military (except those safely away from the front) there was not too much of an appetite for the further fighting and definitely no serious anymosity toward Fritz. Rumyantsev in OTL was quite happy when PIII made peace and Russian #2 general was Fritz’s admirer. It would take very little time for Russia, no matter who was in charge, to figure out that Prussia is more convenient ally than the Hapsburgs. Even under Elizabeth, no matter what the politicians in St.Petersburg were deciding, relations between the Russian and Austrian commanders hd been steadily deteriorating since Kolberg. The Austrians could not reconquer Silesia on their own and the Russian commanders were not willing to keep doing the Austrian job, especially after Doun failed in obligations to provide them with the food and was very cautious in risking the Austrian troops. items.original_question: What if Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg? She lives between a few months to a few years longer in this scenario. Peter III does not withdraw Russian troops from the Seven Years War, the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg does not materialize. Now, nobody was interested in total defeat of Prussia, it would remain a viable country but remains a second rate power in Europe, Silesia would go back to Austria, there would be possibly other territorial concessions as well. What happens to Germany long term in this timeline? Austria obviously becomes the natural candidate for unification of the country but the timeline will likely change.
items.model_answer:
If Empress Elizabeth of Russia had lived longer—long enough to prevent Peter III’s 1762 withdrawal from the Seven Years’ War—Prussia would likely have been defeated. The “Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg,” Russia’s sudden exit from the war after Elizabeth’s death, saved Frederick the Great from near-certain collapse. Without it, the long-term trajectory of Germany would have been fundamentally different.

By early 1762, Prussia was militarily exhausted. Russian and Austrian forces had occupied Berlin briefly in 1760, and Frederick’s resources were nearly spent. If Elizabeth had remained on the throne, Russia would have continued its alliance with Austria, pressing from the east while Austria attacked from the south. Under sustained pressure, Prussia likely would have lost significant territory or been partitioned. Austria probably would have recovered Silesia, the rich province it had lost earlier in the century. Prussia might have been reduced to a secondary north German state, possibly losing influence in Saxony or West Prussia as well.

Without a strengthened Prussia, the German political balance shifts dramatically. The dualism between Austria and Prussia that defined late 18th- and 19th-century German politics would not have developed in the same way. Austria would likely have remained the dominant German power within the Holy Roman Empire and its successor arrangements. The eventual unification of Germany under Prussian leadership in 1871 becomes highly unlikely. Instead, Germany might have evolved into a looser federation under Austrian leadership, or a reformed Habsburg-centered German confederation stretching deep into Central Europe.

The Napoleonic era would also look different. A weakened Prussia would have played a smaller role in resisting Napoleon. Austria, already the major German power, would bear the main burden of opposition. If Austria retained stronger control over German affairs after Napoleon, the German Confederation created in 1815 might have been more cohesive under Habsburg dominance. The idea of a “Lesser Germany” (excluding Austria) would probably never gain traction; a “Greater Germany” including Austria might have been the default path—if unification occurred at all.

Economically, the Zollverein (the Prussian-led customs union that fostered German integration) might not have emerged in its historical form. Without Prussian leadership, economic integration among the German states could have proceeded more slowly or under Austrian guidance, though Austria’s diverse empire might have made coherent economic reform harder. Industrialization in the German lands may still have occurred—given underlying demographic and resource factors—but political consolidation would likely have lagged.

The long-term implications for European power politics are substantial. A Germany unified under Austrian leadership would have been more multinational and internally complex, potentially less centralized and militarized than Bismarck’s Reich. Alternatively, Germany might have remained permanently fragmented into medium-sized states, resembling Italy before unification. In either case, the specific Prusso-German military state that emerged in 1871—shaped by Prussian institutions, Junker dominance, and Bismarckian statecraft—would not exist.

Without the Prussian-led German Empire, the balance of power before World War I changes dramatically. A Habsburg-dominated Central Europe might either be more conservative and multinational, potentially diffusing German nationalism, or more unstable due to ethnic tensions. The particular rivalry between a unified German Empire and Britain or France might never reach the same intensity. While great-power conflict in Europe would still be possible, the path to 1914 would likely look very different.

In sum, if Elizabeth had lived longer and Prussia had been decisively weakened, the rise of a Prussian-led German nation-state becomes improbable. Germany would either unify later under Austrian leadership in a broader, more multinational framework, or remain fragmented. The militarized, industrial great power that emerged in 1871—and shaped European history thereafter—would likely never have taken the same form.

items.question: What If New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani?
human_answers: Yes, really. The social organization was hierarchical and defined by race, as many are even today, with the whites at the top. Again nothing unheard of. It's also true that the Peninsulars were usually assigned the top positions in the Viceroyalties, but even there there were exceptions. Three criollos were viceroys in New Spain and two more in Peru. Apart of that, there was no legal impediment for marriages between whites, mestizos and indios, with the children of such unions considered belonging to the upper class. "Rigid caste systems" never allow marriages outside one's caste and even less allow upwards movement. In many cases, mestizos bribed their way into the white class. Ironically, there were also cases where mestizos bribed their way down to be considered indios, because that put them outside the control from the Inquisition. Black people got it worse, certainly, but even there the social system never reached the hysteric levels of the United States. Intermarriage was complex due to slavery, but still legal. The first registered marriage between a white man and a black woman happened in 1564 in Florida. Of course, the whitest the skin of the children were, the better future they had.

It wouldn't give any advantages to the Spanish, the entire coalition hated the Mexica, keeping him around is not helping them score any points with them. In OTL, the local nobility got incorporated into the Spanish aristocracy, through marriage or by appointment as cacique (lord) of a region. By the Independence War, the most ardent loyalists were the natives, which had the most to lose, together with the Spanish, from a change in government. The enconmienda phase (1500s) was brutal, but by the 1600s, things had settled, and life was back to normal, with a Spanish/Native aristocracy above mestizo and native peasants. The worst abuses to the natives were behind, and the native nobility thrived. Unless there is no total victory, and the Spanish make the the Mexica vassals instead, then they will be in a need for someone to stay in charge. After a few decades, that might even go away if there is a Spanish-Mexica match, the children will be considered Spanish in less than two generations. Unlike the Inca, which I think could survive as a figurehead in Cuzco, the Tlatoani's case is more complicated.
items.original_question: What if New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani? When we think of the Fall of the Aztec Empire, we think of the Spanish coming in and overthrowing the existing order and building New Spain upon the ashes of the Aztec Empire. Well, the answer is a lot more complicated than that thought. One aspect from the Aztec Empire Spain kept was the position of a Tlatoani. Initially, the last sovereign of the Aztec Empire, Cuauhtémoc, was kept alive until Hernan Cortes killed him while bringing along to Honduras. However, Hernan then appointed a person named Tlacotzin (A former advisor of Cuauhtémoc) as tlatoani, (Though he was titled Cuauhtlatoani) but he died the next year before he could return to Tenochtitlan. So, Cortes then appointed a commoner named Motelchiuhtzin net, then he died fighting the Chichimeca up north. Then a man named Xochiquentzin ruled until he died of natural causes. So after that stint, the Spanish appointed Tlatoanis from the previous Aztec dynasty, who were both Tlatoani and Governor of Tenochtitlan (By this point Mexico City) under the Spanish colonial government of New Spain. It started with Panitzin and ended with Cipac. The last one got into frequent disputes over legal issues and disagreements on taxes with the colonial authorities. Afterwards, in just 1565, the Spanish ceased appointing a member of the former dynasty of Tlatoani. But they did continue to appoint a native Judge-governor until Mexican independence in 1821, who were either indigenous or mixed descent and many were descendants of Aztec nobility, though not of the royal dynasty. What if the Spanish continued to appoint continued a blood member of the previous Aztec Empire as "Tlatoani," and continues this until Mexican independence? How would a direct descendent of the Aztec emperors affect the search for a Mexican monarch? Could we see a movement similar to the "Inca Plan" where the Mexicans elect a native Nahuatl as Emperor instead of a European Prince or later Iturbide?
items.model_answer:
If New Spain had continued appointing a tlatoani after the Spanish conquest—maintaining the Aztec imperial title as an official, recognized position within colonial governance—the political and cultural trajectory of central Mexico could have been significantly different.

In the immediate aftermath of conquest, the Spanish initially ruled indirectly through indigenous elites, and the office of tlatoani (the Mexica ruler of Tenochtitlan) survived briefly before being sidelined and replaced by Spanish-style municipal councils (cabildos). If the Spanish Crown had institutionalized the tlatoani as a permanent, crown-sanctioned authority—similar to how it preserved some indigenous nobility in other regions—the result would likely have been a hybrid political system combining imperial Nahua legitimacy with Spanish sovereignty.

Politically, this could have stabilized early colonial rule. A recognized tlatoani, appointed or confirmed by the viceroy but drawn from established noble lineages, would have served as an intermediary between Spanish authorities and Nahua communities. Tribute collection, labor drafts, and religious conversion might have been more effectively organized through an office that carried deep cultural authority. The crown often relied on indigenous nobles anyway; formalizing the tlatoani could have strengthened loyalty while reducing rebellion, particularly in the densely populated Valley of Mexico.

Culturally, the continued presence of a tlatoani would have reinforced Nahua elite identity. Even under Christianization, the symbolic continuity of pre-Hispanic rulership might have preserved more ceremonial, linguistic, and legal traditions at an official level. The tlatoani could have evolved into a Christianized, semi-royal indigenous governor—somewhat analogous to recognized native rulers in parts of the British Empire centuries later. Nahuatl literacy, pictorial codices, and courtly traditions might have retained higher prestige for longer, potentially slowing the cultural marginalization of indigenous political forms.

However, there would also have been tensions. Spanish settlers and peninsular elites might have resisted granting too much authority to a figure rooted in a pre-conquest imperial ideology. Over time, the tlatoani’s power would almost certainly have become ceremonial, constrained by Spanish law, clergy, and the viceroy. If the office retained too much symbolic autonomy, it might have become a rallying point for anti-colonial movements, especially during crises like epidemics, famine, or Bourbon reforms.

In the long term, the existence of a continuous tlatoani could have reshaped Mexican national identity. At independence in the nineteenth century, reformers might have drawn on that surviving indigenous monarchy as a constitutional symbol—perhaps producing a syncretic monarchy rooted in both Aztec and Spanish traditions rather than the short-lived European-backed empire of Iturbide or Maximilian. Indigenous political legitimacy might have occupied a more central place in national narratives much earlier.

In short, if New Spain had kept appointing a tlatoani, colonial rule in central Mexico would likely have been more visibly hybrid and institutionally plural. Indigenous elite continuity would have been stronger, cultural erosion slower at the top levels of society, and Mexico’s later political imagination potentially more rooted in an unbroken pre-Hispanic sovereign tradition.

items.question: What If Almanzor had never risen to power in al-Andalus?
human_answers: I had to read about Ghalib because my knowledge of him is quite limited. Overall, he seems to be a competent Saqaliba (slave-soldier) leader and served three caliphs. I don't see why he would try to reshape the composition of the caliphate as Al-Mansur did when trying to use Berbers against the rest of Islamic Iberia. Ghālib's rise coincides with the retirement of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III from active military command following his defeat at the Battle of Simancas in 939. So he came to serve under the first caliph and had a life of distinguished service fighting against Vikings, Moroccans, Fatimids, and Christians from northern Iberia. Gaining his freedom and patronage from the Umayyad. Perhaps it will have a greater influence from the Saqaliba in general within the caliphate. But to be honest, overall, they were good slave soldiers, and in the OTL, when the caliphate began to collapse, they were the ones who desperately fought against the Berbers to try to keep the caliphate alive and prevent the sackings of the city of Córdoba. I think one factor that made them generally better managers than the Mamluks in Egypt was that the ṣaqāliba were much less institutionalized and more integrated into local society. This was largely because Andalusian power was always balanced by military pluralism. With Arabs, Berbers, local Andalusians (the Muwallads), Ṣaqāliba, and Christian mercenaries, this balance prevented a single military group from monopolizing the state, as the Mamluks had done. So a Mameluke is freed to never cease being a Mameluke, while a ṣaqāliba is freed to cease being a ṣaqāliba. I'd guess that overall, you have a continuation of the status quo of the period, with a normal caliph (not the puppets of the period). There will be ethnic tensions that rise and fall depending on the situation, disputes over spheres of influence, campaigns in North Africa against the Fatimids (and in the future the Berber caliphates if they rise to power), and campaigns against Christians in the north (Kingdom of Leon), which may or may not succeed depending on the general, as happened in the OTL. It's difficult to say whether this prevents the reconquest of Iberia, but it certainly prevents the implosion of the caliphate of OTL. I would say that what will have the greatest impact on the survival of the Caliphate is not the Christians in the north, but rather the possible rise of the Almoravids.

I think that after ibn Abi Amir is killed, Ghalib is hailed as a hero by the Arab ruling class. As hajib, the old general, committed to the survival of the Caliphate as an institution, would free Hisham II from his irrelevance and perhaps have advisors train the boy-Caliph for rule. Once he reaches the age of maturity, Hisham takes power, albeit he mostly delegates authority to capable bureaucrats. His rule might be an extension of his father’s, a time of peace and prosperity and a golden age of the arts and sciences. The Christians are still too disorganized and weak to push into al-Andalus. Sancho III of Navarre is likely never even born as a result of butterflies. So no Jimenez dynasty either. Christian Spain remains small and disunited while Cordoba remains quietly strong and prosperous. I agree, the real threat to Cordoba wouldn’t be from the north, but from the south.
